canonical_question: Is the '1073 K' heating temperature of the unirradiated part of the APT needle representative of peak temperatures expected in a nuclear reactor?

question_variants.question: Is the '1073 K' heating temperature of the unirradiated part of the APT needle representative of peak temperatures expected in a nuclear reactor?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text states the unirradiated part of the APT needle was heated to 1073 K during the irradiation of the other part. The document does not explicitly state whether this temperature is representative of peak temperatures in a nuclear reactor, nor does it define the 'peak' temperature regime.

answers.answer: The APT needle extracted from the irradiated sample contained two parts: deep unirradiated, but heated to 1073 K and an irradiated part at 1073 K.
answers.boundary_limitation: No comparison to nuclear reactor peak temperatures is made in the text
evidence_spans: The average hardness of the unirradiated sample was measured to be 13.25 GPa.
After annealing the sample hardness increased to 16.25 GPa, while after irradiation the sample hardness reached a value of 20 GPa.

Increase in hardness after annealing is solely associated with Hf segregation along the GBs whereas the increase after irradiation is a synergistic combination between Ar implantation, lattice distortion caused by irradiation ballistic mixing, and grain refinement.
